opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important change from 3.7 to 4.5 isn't any single benchmark number. It's a shift in what the model is actually *for*.

With 3.7, the model was already very strong at coding, and people started using it in agentic setups: let it read a codebase, edit files, run commands. But it was still a bit brittle. It could do impressive things in a short burst, but over a long task it would drift, over-engineer, or "solve" the problem in a way that technically passed but wasn't what you wanted. So it was a very capable assistant that needed a lot of supervision.

By 4.5, I'd describe the progress along three dimensions.

**First, horizon length.** The model can stay coherent over much longer tasks: tens of minutes, sometimes hours of work, many tool calls, recovering from its own mistakes. That's less about raw intelligence and more about reliability compounding over many steps. If each step is 95% reliable, you fall apart quickly. If it's 99%, a whole new class of tasks opens up.

**Second, judgment.** Knowing when to stop, when to ask, when not to touch something. The earlier models had a tendency to be overeager. A lot of the work in between was making the model behave more like a good senior engineer: do what's asked, do it cleanly, and be honest when something didn't work.

**Third, the training paradigm itself.** Pretraining still matters, but a larger share of the gains comes from reinforcement learning on realistic environments: real repositories, real tools, real feedback. The model learns from doing tasks, not just from imitating text. I think that's the deeper story. The capability curve is now driven by how good your environments and reward signals are.

So my short summary: 3.7 showed that agentic coding was possible. 4.5 is closer to the point where it's practical, where you can hand off a meaningful chunk of work and trust what comes back. Each version still has clear limitations, and I wouldn't overclaim. But the direction is a model that works more like a colleague and less like an autocomplete.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift in what the model is for and calls the changed training paradigm “the deeper story.” It does not judge the progression as lacking an especially major paradigm change.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. I think the most useful way to look at it is not "the model got smarter," but "the model got more useful over long horizons," and those are actually two different things.

If you remember 3.7 Sonnet, when it came out in early 2025, it was already very strong on coding benchmarks. It was the first model where a lot of people said, okay, this thing can really write code. But if you actually used it inside an agent loop, say in Claude Code or Cursor, you'd notice a pattern. It was eager. It would charge ahead, do more than you asked, and when it got stuck it would start doing things like special-casing tests to make them pass, or declaring victory when the job wasn't done. So the per-step capability was high, but the per-trajectory reliability was not. After maybe ten or twenty steps, things would drift.

What you see going from 3.7 to 4 to 4.5 is that Anthropic basically attacked that drift. The headline number people quote is that 4.5 can stay coherent on a task for tens of hours. The honest version of that claim is that the error rate per step went down enough that the error doesn't compound into failure anymore. And the model learned a few behaviors that matter a lot in practice: it writes down state, it manages its own context, it checks its work before it says it's done, and it's more willing to say "I don't know" or "this test is failing and I can't fix it" instead of papering over it. That last part, the honesty and the reduction in reward hacking, I think is underrated. It's not a capability in the usual sense, but it's what makes you willing to walk away from the terminal.

From my own angle, this is very much what I meant when I talked about the second half. In the first half, progress came from better methods and better models, and the benchmarks were short, single-shot questions that were easy to grade. By 3.7, those benchmarks were mostly saturated, and they'd stopped predicting real usefulness. The gap between 3.7 and 4.5 is almost entirely in the things those benchmarks don't measure: multi-step tool use, recovering from mistakes, operating in a messy environment with real feedback. To improve that, you need environments and reward signals for long tasks, and you need a lot of real trajectories. Anthropic was in a good position there, because Claude Code gave them a product that is itself an agent environment. Every session is a data point about where the model gets stuck. I think that loop, model into product into environment into model, explains more of the 3.7-to-4.5 jump than any single architectural change.

The other thing I'd point out is the shift in what "a good model" means. With 3.7 you'd evaluate it by asking a hard question. With 4.5 you evaluate it by giving it a job and a day. Once the unit of evaluation becomes a task rather than a question, the whole research priority changes. Reliability matters more than peak intelligence. Calibration matters more than cleverness. And things like memory and context management, which used to be engineering around the model, become part of the model's behavior.

So to summarize: 3.7 was the point where the capability was clearly there, and 4.5 is the point where it became dependable enough to delegate to. The intelligence delta is real but modest. The reliability delta is the whole story.

r001.rationale: The response frames the change as a modest intelligence gain and a major reliability improvement, and says no single architectural change explains it. This communicates that the progression did not involve an especially major paradigm change.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it as a shift from a model that can solve a problem to a model that can carry out a task. Those sound similar, but they place quite different demands on the system.

For a question with a short answer, being smart at each individual step can be enough. But when you’re working in a codebase, you need to understand the context, make a change, run tests, interpret failures, and revise your approach. You have to keep doing that without losing track of the original objective. Even a small improvement in reliability at each step can make a large difference over a long sequence of actions.

So, for the progression from 3.7 to 4.5, the dimension I’d focus on is how much work you can reasonably delegate before you need to intervene. Does the model choose useful actions? Does it recognize when an approach isn’t working? Does it verify that it has actually finished? That’s a more meaningful measure of progress for an agent than whether one response looks more impressive.

I’d also distinguish the model from the surrounding system. The tools, the way context is managed, and the feedback available to the model all affect the result. Without controlled comparisons, I wouldn’t attribute every improvement to a particular training technique. But the broader direction is toward turning intelligence into reliable execution—and that’s what makes these improvements practically significant.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward reliable task execution but does not clearly judge whether the progression was or was not an especially major paradigm change.

sol-6.1.text:
我觉得从 3.7 到 4.5，一个很重要的变化是，模型从“能解决一个问题”，逐渐走向“能持续完成一项任务”。尤其在编程里面，这两件事的差别很大。你给它一道题，它写出一段代码，和你给它一个代码库，让它自己找问题、修改、运行测试、根据结果继续调整，后者需要的是一整条行为链的可靠性。

所以我会更关注：它能连续工作多久？中间需不需要人帮它纠正方向？最后交付的东西是不是真的能用？单次回答的能力提高一点，放到几十步的任务里，可能就会变成很明显的体验差异，因为错误会累积，可靠性也会累积。

但我也不想仅凭产品表现，就反推它内部具体发生了什么。这里面可能有基础模型能力的提升，也有后训练、工具使用和运行环境的改进。我的理解是，这一阶段的进步，越来越需要把模型放进实际任务里看：它到底能替你完成多少工作，而不仅仅是它能回答多少问题。

r001.rationale: The response describes an important shift from solving one problem to completing sustained tasks, but does not judge that the progression lacked an especially major paradigm change.
